Act One.

(At the conclusion of the benediction, the Stage Manager enters. Stage Manager: (Note: The stage direction "nāndyante" indicates the end of the traditional invocation or benediction performed at the beginning of a Sanskrit drama. "Sūtradhāraḥ" refers to the director or Stage Manager who traditionally opens the performance.)
May he who struck down Gādhiputra and the obstructors of the sacrifice; who slew Virādha and destroyed the prowess of Khara and Dūṣaṇa in battle;
who killed the arrogant and fierce Kabandha and the lord of monkeys; and who is the slayer of the race of the lords of night-rangers—may he protect you all.
Thus I inform the noble sirs.
(Walking about and looking around) Ah! While I am occupied in making this request, what is this sound that is heard? Dear friend, let me see.
(Offstage) Sugrīva! This way, this way!
(Entering)
The Attendant:
My Lord, from where indeed has this great sound arisen, which resounds so loudly as to tear the ears?
Like clouds thundering in the sky, moving with a terrifying speed as they were driven by a fierce wind. || 2 ||

Sūtradhāra:—My friend, do you not understand? Indeed, this is the undertaking that has commenced to slay Vālin, the lord of all monkeys, who wears a golden garland, by Rāma—the lamp of the Raghu dynasty, who causes distress through the abduction of Sītā, and who is pleasing to the eyes of all the world—and by Sugrīva, the king of all bears and monkeys, whose great neck is so massive, and who has been deprived of his realm because his wife was violated; both having made a mutual promise to assist one another. Therefore, come, let us proceed.
Now Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa have arrived to restore Sugrīva, who has been deprived of his kingdom,
just as Hari and Hara restored Indra.
(Both exit.
The prologue ends.
(Then Rāma enters, along with Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva, and Hanumān.)
Rāma:
Sugrīva, this way, this way!
Today, with my arrows, I shall suddenly strike down upon the earth your enemy, whose body has been slain, pierced, and scattered.
O King! Cast away your fear; you have seen him standing near me, and that Vālī has been slain by you in battle. || 4 ||
Sugrīva: My Lord! By the grace of my noble brother, I consider even the sovereignty of the gods within my reach, let alone that of the monkeys. For why?
O Lord! Released today by you, there is no doubt in my mind that I shall pierce the heart of Vālin.

O Śrīdhara! Having pierced seven *sāla* trees in the great forest of the snowy mountain that resembles a peak, and having entered the earth with the force of its momentum, this arrow has now returned after traveling to the abode of the *nāgas* and plunging again into the ocean, O Hero! (5)
Hanumān:
O King! By the words issuing from your mouth, we are indeed freed from fear and our grief has vanished.
O best of the Raghus! Go toward the mountain, which resembles a water-laden cloud, to grant victory to Hari.
Lakṣmaṇa:

Noble brother! Because of its lushness, Kiṣkindhā must surely be situated all around the interior of the forest. Sugrīva: [Laughs] Noble brother, you have spoken well. It is indeed so. For this very reason, we shall proceed toward Kiṣkindhā. Now, having reached the mountain peak, look at the city of Kiṣkindhā, which is like a second Amarāvatī. Here, the mountain, with its peaks adorned by the rays of the rising sun, appears as if it were the eastern quarter itself. And here, the western quarter, bearing the splendor of the setting sun, seems as if it were the very abode of the Lord of the Dead (Yama). Furthermore, the southern quarter, marked by the presence of the sun’s rays, appears as if it were the very mouth of the God of Death. And here, the northern quarter, possessing the beauty of the moon, shines forth as if it were the very abode of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera). Moreover, the sky, filled with the rays of the sun, appears as if it were the very abode of the Lord of the Gods (Indra). The prince has spoken rightly.
O King, Kiṣkindhā has been reached, protected by the arms of the best of monkeys—protected by your own arms.
Stay here, O best of men! I shall render the world of men unconscious with my roar, making even the mountains tremble.
Rāma: Very well, go. Sugrīva: [He departs.]
"As Your Majesty commands. (Walking around) O Lord! Though abandoned by you without any specific offense being cited, Sugrīva desires to perform service at your feet in battle.
(Offstage) What? Sugrīva?
(Then enters Vālī together with Tārā, who holds his garment.)
Bali: What? Sugrīva?
Tārā! O lady of faultless limbs, release my garment!
O you with drooping face and eyes! Why have you set out?
Behold Sugrīva today being struck down in battle, his entire body drenched in blood.
Tārā:
"May the Great King be gracious, may he be gracious! Sugrīva will not come for such a trivial reason. Therefore, you must go after consulting with the circle of ministers.
Bālin:
Ah,
O moon-faced one! Whether it be Śakra who is my refuge, or Śiva with his sharpened battle-axe against my enemy!
Neither Viṣṇu, with his eyes like blooming white lotuses, nor anyone else, is capable of striking me when he comes before my face.
Tārā:
"May the Great King be gracious, may he be gracious! It behooves the Great King to grant favor to this person.
Bālin:
Listen to my prowess, O Tārā!
Indeed, in the past, during the churning for the nectar of immortality, I went there and, laughing, looked upon the hosts of gods, dānavas, and daityas;
they were utterly amazed as they beheld the lord of serpents, of fierce form, with eyes wide open, being dragged away. 11.9.
Tārā:
"Be gracious, be gracious, O Great King!
Bālī: [listens]
Āḥ! Be obedient to my will! Enter within.
Tārā: Here I go, unfortunate as I am. (She exits. Here I go, unfortunate as I am.
Bali:
Ah, Tārā has entered! Now I shall break Sugrīva’s neck! (Approaching swiftly) Sugrīva! Stop, stop!
Let Indra be your refuge, or let the Lord Madhusūdana be your protector!
Having come within the range of my sight, you shall not depart alive.
This way, this way!
Sugrīva: As the Great King commands.
(Both engage in hand-to-hand combat.
Rāma:
Here he is, here is Bālin!
With his lips bitten together, his fierce eyes bloodshot, and his fangs bared with a tightly clenched fist,
the monkey roars terribly in battle, shining like the fire of universal destruction desiring to consume all.
Lakṣmaṇa:
Let my noble brother also behold Sugrīva—
his eyes as red as blooming lotuses, his thick arms bound with golden armlets.
Having abandoned the conduct of the virtuous and overcome his elder, he approaches the best of monkeys because of his monkey-nature.
Struck by Vālin, Sugrīva fell.
Hanumān—Alas! Woe!
(Approaching Rāma with agitation) Victory to the Lord! Such is her condition;
the lord of the monkeys is powerful, yet my husband is weak.
The situation and the oath itself—let all this be considered by the noble one.
Rāma:— Hanuman! Enough, enough with this agitation! This is being carried out. (Releasing the arrow) Ah, Bālin has fallen!
Lakṣmaṇa:—
There he is, that very Bālin—his limbs smeared with blood, his reddened eyes rolling, his firm and massive arms outstretched, desiring to enter the realm of Death.
With his momentum stilled, though enveloped by a shower of arrows, he somehow falls forward, slowly dragging along his body. (16)
Bali—(Fainting, then regaining his composure and reading the letters of the name upon the arrow, addressing Rāma:
O Rāma! It is fitting for one established in the duty of a king to deceive me in battle by such unrighteous means!
By the Hero, who has removed all doubt regarding the Dharma and is intent on dispelling the delusions of the worlds. || 17 ||
Alas, sir! By you, who possess such a gentle appearance and are a vessel of glory, deep-rooted infamy has been created by striking me through deceit. (18)
O Raghava! For me, who am intent on battle with my brother—who wears bark garments and whose mind is distracted by his altered appearance—a hidden killing would indeed be unrighteous.
Rama:
How so? Why would a hidden killing be unrighteous?
Bālin: What doubt could there be?
Rāma:—
This is certainly not so. Behold:
the slaughter of deer is desired by relying on a concealed snare;
because you are both a deer and one who ought to be slain, you have been punished by means of a concealment. (19)
Bali: You consider me to be one who deserves punishment.
Rāma:
What doubt is there?
Bālin: For what reason?
Rāma:
By approaching one who should not be approached.
Bālī: [What of it?]
"By approaching one who should not be approached—this is our duty.
Rāma:
"But surely, sir, this is improper!"
By you, the lord of monkeys, who discerns between dharma and adharma, the violation of your brother’s wife was committed for the sake of a deer. (20)
Bāli:
"I alone have been punished, and not Sugrīva, even though our offenses were equal through the violation of my brother's wife.
Rāma: [listens].
For you have been punished because you deserved punishment; one who does not deserve punishment is never punished.
Bālin—my preceptor’s lawful wife was violated by Sugrīva.
O Raghava, how can I be punished for violating his wife?

Rāma: But such a thing as the violation of an elder brother's wife by a younger brother has never occurred. Bālin: [Laughs] Indeed! How could it be otherwise? For you, O Rāma, are the very embodiment of righteousness (dharma). What other man would ever dare to speak thus? Even the gods themselves would be terrified of you. You are the son of Daśaratha, the scion of the Raghu dynasty, and the slayer of Khara. You have performed the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) and are the protector of the world. You are the one who slew the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the destroyer of the demons. You are the one who rescued Sītā from the mouth of the sea-monster (Jatayu), and you are the one who destroyed the city of Laṅkā. You are the one who slew the demon Tāḍaka, the subduer of the sons of Pulastya, and the one who crushed the pride of the Nivātakavaca demons. You are the one who killed the son of Virocana, the slayer of the demon Kumbhakarṇa, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Rākṣasas. You are the one who slew the son of Bali, the conqueror of the three cities (Tripura), and the one who destroyed the pride of the Asuras. You are the one who killed the son of Jambha, the slayer of the demon Naraka, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Daityas. You are the one who slew the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Dānavas. You are the one who killed the son of Śambara, the slayer of the demon Bāṇa, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Yakṣas. You are the one who slew the son of Mura, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Guhyakas. You are the one who killed the son of Andhaka, the slayer of the demon Śumbha, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Rakshasas. You are the one who slew the son of Prahlada, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Asuras. You are the one who killed the son of Vipracitti, the slayer of the demon Namuci, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Danavas. You are the one who slew the son of Śakuni, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Gandharvas. You are the one who killed the son of Maya, the slayer of the demon Bala, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Panis. You are the one who slew the son of Vritra, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Daityas. You are the one who killed the son of Namuchi, the slayer of the demon Hayagriva, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Asuras. You are the one who slew the son of Śambara, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Dānavas. You are the one who killed the son of Hiranyaksha, the slayer of the demon Naraka, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Daityas. You are the one who slew the son of Bali, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Asuras. You are the one who slew the son of Maya, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Panis. You are the one who killed the son of Andhaka, the slayer of the demon Shumbha, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Rakshasas. You are the one who slew the son of Prahlada, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Asuras. You are the one who slew the son of Shakuni, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the one who destroyed the pride of the Gandharvas. You are the one who killed the son of Maya
Ah, we are now unsurpassed! Since I have been punished by you, am I not indeed freed from sin?
Rāma: So be it.
Sugrīva: Alas, what a tragedy!
O you who walk with the gait of a lordly elephant, your two arms, which resemble the trunks of elephants and whose armlets have been mangled by the weapons of your enemies—
O best of monkeys, seeing your two arms resting upon the surface of the earth, my heart today seems as if it is falling! || 22 ||
Bali:
Sugrīva! Enough, enough with this despondency; such is the way of the world.
(Behind the scenes:)
Alas, alas, Great King!
Bālin:
Sugrīva! Let the women be restrained, let them be restrained! They ought not to see me in such a state.
Sugrīva: As the Great King commands. Hanumān, let it be done so. Hanumān: [Does as instructed].
"As the prince commands.
(Exit. (Then enter Aṅgada and Hanumān.)
Hanumān:
Aṅgada! This way, this way! Aṅgada: [Approaches]
Having heard that Hari, the lord of the hosts of bears, was succumbing to the power of time,
I am overcome with grief and proceed with faltering steps.
Hanuman! Where is the great king?
Hanuman:
Here is the great king.
With his heart pierced by arrows, he shone upon the surface of the earth like the excellent mountain Krauñca when assailed by the power of Guha. || 24 ||
Aṅgada: (Approaching) Alas, Great King!
Formerly, the Lord of Monkeys was accustomed to sleeping in profound ease.
Lying upon the surface of the earth, with all movement of your limbs exhausted, having clearly cast off your body pierced by the enemy's arrows— O hero, do you now desire to go to heaven? (25)
(Falling to the ground) Bālin:
Enough, enough with this despondency! O Sugrīva!
Having set aside with your intellect the fault committed by me, O Lord of the Monkeys, you should properly cast off your anger, embrace righteousness, and uphold this sprout of our lineage. (23)
Sugrīva: As the Great King commands.
Vālī:
"O Raghava! For whatever offense you may choose to forgive this monkey's fickleness.
Rama: "Certainly."
Bali: Sugrīva! Please accept this golden necklace, the ancestral treasure of my family.
Rāma: [Silence]
I am favored. (He accepts.
Bālin:
Hanūman! Fetch some water, then.
Hanumān:
As the Great King commands. (Exiting and re-entering) Here is water.
Bālin:

(Having sipped water) My vital breaths seem to be deserting me. These great rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, and these celestial nymphs, beginning with Urvaśī, have come to me. Here is that hero-bearing celestial chariot, yoked with a thousand swans, sent by Time and arrived to take me away. Very well; here I come. (He ascends to heaven.
All:
Alas, alas, Great King!
Rāma:
Alas, Vālī has gone to heaven! Sugrīva, let his funeral rites be performed. Sugrīva:—
"As the King commands.
Rāma:
"Lakṣmaṇa! Let the consecration of Sugrīva be prepared."
Lakṣmaṇa: As my noble brother commands.
(All exit.)
The first act is finished. (Then enters Kakubha.
Kakubha:

"Since the task is almost completed, all the monkey leaders are occupied with eating; therefore, I too shall prepare some kind of food. (He does so. (Entering) Bilamukha: The task is nearly finished, so all the monkey leaders are occupied with eating; therefore, I too shall prepare some kind of food. (He does so.
(Entering) Bilamukha:

I have been sent by the great lord Sugrīva to return the favor of the noble Rāma; all the monkeys have been dispatched to every quarter, and they have returned. Having learned news of Prince Aṅgada, who set out toward the southern path, [Sugrīva] said, "Come back quickly. So, where indeed has the prince gone? (Walking about and looking ahead) Here is the noble Kauhaka. I shall ask him. (Approaching) Is it well with the noble sir?

"I have been sent by the great king Sugrīva for the sake of repaying the favor done to noble Rāma. All the monkeys dispatched to search for Sītā in every direction have returned. Having learned news of Prince Aṅgada, who set out toward the southern region, they told me, 'He should return quickly. But where indeed has the prince gone? Here is Āryaka-kubha; I shall ask him. Is the noble one well?
Kubha:
Ah, Bilamukha! From where do you come?
Bilamukha:
Noble sir! By the command of the Great King, I have come to see Prince Aṅgada. Kakubha:—
"Is the noble Rāma and the great king Bilamukha well?"—
"Yes."
Kakubha:
What is the intention of the Great King? (Bilamukha recites as before: "I have been sent. Kakubha: ...
"Do you not know that half of the task is already accomplished?
Bilāmukha— "What? What?"
Kakubha:
Listen— having learned the news of Rāma’s wife from the king of birds,
Vāyuputra has today leaped across the ocean by virtue of his superior prowess, having mounted Airāvata, the lord of elephants, and Mahendra, the lord of mountains, to reach Laṅkā swiftly.
Therefore, come; let us both take refuge at the very feet of the prince. (They both exit. Interlude. (Then enters Sītā, surrounded by a host of Rākṣasa women.
Sītā:

Alas! I am indeed pitiless and ill-fated, for though separated from my noble husband and brought to the palace of the Rākṣasa king, I still live—this unfortunate one—enduring unwanted and undeserved words uttered according to his whims. Or rather, through the conviction that my noble husband is alive, I somehow sustain myself. But why is it that today, while the circle of sacrificial fires is being kindled, even a slight cooling sensation has arisen from the region of my heart?

"Could it be that my noble husband’s heart is now turned toward me? (Alas! Shame! I am truly too steadfast for one so ill-fated. Separated from my noble husband and brought to the palace of the Rākṣasa king, I yet live—though I am told of these undesirable and undeserved events unfolding exactly contrary to my wishes, I, unfortunate as I am, continue to draw breath. Or rather, by means of the conviction that my noble husband is still alive, I somehow sustain myself."

"What indeed is this sudden clarity of heart that has arisen, like a sprinkling of water, while the circle of fire for the executioners is being kindled today? Could it be that my noble son’s heart has become clear toward me?
Hanumān—(entering Laṅkā)—Oh, what a magnificent layout of Rāvaṇa’s palace!

Lanka shines like the city of Mahendra in the sky, rich with ornate gateways fashioned of gold and adorned in places with excellent jewels and coral, and filled with spotless, magnificent celestial chariots.
Alas! Having obtained this unsurpassed royal fortune, the Ten-necked one, because he has set out upon a wrong path, is now intent on destroying it. (3)

(Having gone everywhere) I have searched almost all of Laṅkā—repeatedly in the inner apartments, the courtyards, the halls, and the palaces; in the bath-houses, the mansions of the Lord of Night-stalkers, the temples, and the towers; in the taverns, the private chambers, and the recesses—I have traversed it all! Alas! I have searched everything, yet the King’s wife is not to be seen by me.

"Alas, my exertion has been in vain! Very well; let me climb to the top of this palace wall and look out. (Having done so) "Ah, here is the grove of the pleasure-garden. I shall enter it and investigate. (Entering and looking around) "Oh, the splendor of this pleasure-grove!

For here, with its regions made variegated by rows of great trees fashioned from gold, coral, and sapphires, this most beautiful mountain shines white, resembling a celestial playground in the sky. (5)
Moreover, I have seen mountains beautiful with veins of gold flowing like variegated streams; I have seen ponds adorned by various water-faring birds;
and I have seen regions always filled with trees rich in flowers and fruit. Indeed, all this has been seen by me in Rāvaṇa’s house, yet Sītā has not been seen by me.
Who indeed is this that appears as if radiant in this region? I shall look there for a moment. (Having done so) Ah! Who can this be?
This woman of slender waist, surrounded by hideous ogresses, shines like a streak of lightning situated amidst dark clouds. (7)
She who wears a single braid like a black serpent, whose waist is measured by the span of a hand, whose heart is fixed on her beloved;
her body emaciated by fasting and her face drenched with tears, she is like a lotus-forest garland cast away in the heat of the sun.
Ah, how is it that there is the light of a lamp? (Looking) Ah, it is Rāvaṇa!

With his crown set with jewels, his beautiful, copper-hued, and long eyes, walking with the graceful gait of one in rut, possessing the majesty of an elephant in musth—this Lord of the Rākṣasas shines amidst the multitude of young women like a lion moving among a herd of does. (9)

What shall I do now? Very well, I have seen a way. I will climb this Ashoka tree and, concealing myself within a hollow, learn the truth of the matter firmly. (He does so. (Then enters Rāvaṇa with his retinue.
Rāvaṇa:

[Addressing himself]—I am Rāvaṇa, who in battle routed the armies of the gods, Daityas, and Dānavas with celestial weapons, and whose chest was struck by the thunderbolt of the enraged Indra, yet remained unharmed.

"Sītā, lacking discernment, does not take pleasure in me; rather, that lovely-eyed woman is surely attached to a lowly ascetic of the Kṣatriya caste—alas, what a frustrating obstacle wrought by fate! (10)

(Looking upward) Here he is, here is the moon, shining like a mirror wrought of silver; expanding in the sky, the moon—the dear kinsman of the beds of night-lotuses—rises, filling my heart with longing with his clusters of rays. (11)

(Walking about) Here is Sītā, seated at the foot of a tree with her heart shrouded in meditation, her face emaciated by fasting; as if wishing to enter her own body, her breasts and belly are closely drawn together, like a crescent moon obscured by storm clouds, she sits surrounded by a host of Rākṣasīs.
She who, having cast aside pleasures, me, and this great prosperity—
Though her heart was fixed upon a mortal, she did not at all come under his control.
Hanumān:
Ah, well understood! This is that princess of Mithilā, the wife of Rāma;
terrified by the sight of the lion, she suffers like a doe.
Rāvaṇa:
(Approaching) Sītā! Abandon this vow of fierce asceticism; O beautiful lady, accept me with all your limbs!
"O blessed lady, having cast aside today that mortal man whose life has ended and who has turned away from the path of desire," || 14 ||
Sītā:
Rāvaṇa is indeed laughable, he who does not even know the power inherent in his own words.
Hanumān—
(With anger) Oh, what arrogance on the part of Rāvaṇa!
He did not recognize those two arms, nor even that exceedingly great bow.
And it speaks of Rāma’s arrow as well, saying, "Its life has departed. || 15 ||
I am unable to restrain my anger. Very well; I myself shall accomplish the task for the noble Rāma.
Or rather, if I slay Rāvaṇa, the purpose will be achieved.

"As the noble one commands. (Walking about) Ah, it is Vibhīṣaṇa! Vibhīṣaṇa! Are you well?
Vibhīṣaṇa:
Ah, it is Prince Lakṣmaṇa! Prince! Today I have become well indeed.
Lakṣmaṇa:—Vibhīṣaṇa! Let us then approach the noble one.
Vibhīṣaṇa:— [Approaches]
Very well.
(As they approach) Lakṣmaṇa:
Victory to the Noble One!
Vibhīṣaṇa:
May the Lord be gracious; may the Lord be victorious!
Rāma:
Ah, it is Vibhīṣaṇa! Vibhīṣaṇa! Are you well? Vibhīṣaṇa:—
"O King! Today I have become well.
Having come for refuge to you, whose eyes are like lotus petals and who are the protector, I am today well, O King, my sins cleansed by the sight of you. (11)
Rāma:
From this day forward, by my command, become the Lord of Laṅkā.
Vibhīṣaṇa: [Accepts.]
I am favored. Rāma:—Vibhīṣaṇa! By your arrival alone, our task is accomplished; for indeed, no means has been found for crossing the ocean.
Vibhīṣaṇa:
My Lord, what is to be understood here? If he does not grant passage, Your Majesty ought to discharge a divine weapon at the ocean.
Rāma:—
Excellent, Vibhīṣaṇa! Excellent! Very well, I shall do as you say. (Rising suddenly with indignation:
My lake has its mud and water scorched by my arrows, and its surface strewn with hundreds of slain fish.
If he does not grant me this path,
I shall quickly make him roar with obstructed waves.
(Then Varuṇa enters.
Varuṇa — (With agitation:)
Having committed an offense against the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who had assumed a human form for the sake of a specific purpose,
he fled swiftly from the one who destroys the bodies of the enemies of the gods.
Terrified, I take refuge in him as my protection from the arrow. || 13 ||
(Looking) Ah, here is the Blessed One,
who, having assumed a human form and bearing the discus, the Śārṅga bow, and the mace,
has arrived himself as the cause, seeking the fulfillment of his purpose.
Homage to the Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa, the cause of the three worlds!
Lakṣmaṇa:
(Looking) Ah, who indeed might this be?
With a crown fashioned of jewels, beautiful and large copper-colored eyes, dark as a fresh blue lotus, and possessing the grace of an elephant in rut—
this one has quickly risen from the midst of the mass of waters.
He seemed to make the world of living beings bow down before him with his splendor. || 15 ||
Vibhīṣaṇa:— My Lord! This is indeed the blessed Varuṇa who has arrived.
Rāma:—
"Is this Varuṇa? O Blessed One! Varuṇa! Salutations to you!
Varuṇa:
"The Lord of the Gods ought not to offer salutations to me. Or rather,"
O Prince! From where does this anger arise? Why is there such wrath in you?
O best of men, tell us quickly what must be done by us. (16)
Rāma:
You ought to grant me passage for my journey to Laṅkā.
Varuṇa: [Agrees.]
"This is the way. May you proceed. (He disappears.
Rāma:
How has the venerable Varuṇa disappeared? Vibhīṣaṇa! Look, look at the Lord of Waters, whose waves have become motionless through the grace of the Blessed One!
Vibhīṣaṇa:
O Lord, at present the ocean appears as if it has split in two.
Rāma: [Listens.]
Where is Hanumān? Hanumān—
Victory to the Lord!
Rāma:
Hanumān, go ahead. Hanumān: [Does so.]
"As the King commands.

Rāma:

(Looking with astonishment) Dear Lakṣmaṇa! Friend Vibhīṣaṇa! Great King Sugrīva! Friend Hanumān! Behold, behold, sirs! Oh, how wondrous is the ocean! For here indeed, in one place it belches forth foam, and in another its waters are teeming with fish.

In some places it is strewn with conch shells, and in others it resembles dark blue clouds; in some places it is garlanded with waves, and in others it is terrifying with crocodiles; in some places it has fearsome whirlpools, and in others its waters are perfectly still.
"By the grace of the Blessed One, the ocean has been crossed.
Hanumān—O Lord! Here, here is Laṅkā."
Rāma—
(Gazing for a long time) Ah, the splendor of this city of Rākṣasas shall soon perish,
shattered by the falling gale of my excellent arrows.
Struck at its edge by the waves of the army of excellent elephants,
it falls down like a ship upon the waters of the ocean that has met with disaster due to the fault of Rāvaṇa as its helmsman. 18.
Sugrīva! Let the army encamp on this Suvela mountain. (They sit down.
Sugrīva: As the Lord commands. Nīla! Let it be done accordingly.
(Entering) Nīla:

As the Great King commands. (Exiting and re-entering) Victory to the Lord! While the armies are being stationed in their respective order and the troop formations are being verified according to the authority of the registers—
Two forest-dwellers, whose origins are unknown, have been captured. We do not know what should be done; therefore, Your Majesty is the authority.
Rāma:—Let these two be brought in quickly.
Nīla:
As the Lord commands. (Exit.

The monkeys:
Alas! Speak! Who are you? (Alas! Speak! Who are you two?
Both:
"Master! We are the servants of Noble Kumuda.
The Monkeys:
"Master! They represent themselves as the servants of Noble Kumuda."
Vibhīṣaṇa:—
(Looking attentively at Śuka and Sāraṇa) These two are not my own soldiers, nor are they forest-dwellers.
"These two Rākṣasas, Śuka and Sāraṇa, have been sent by Rāvaṇa."

Both—(To themselves) Ah, we have been recognized by the prince! (Aloud) Noble sir! Having seen the race of Rākṣasas perishing through the misconduct of the king of the Rākṣasas, and finding no refuge, we two have arrived in the form of monkeys for the sake of seeking your protection.
Rāma: Friend Vibhīṣaṇa, what do you think?
Vibhīṣaṇa:—
"O King! These two are indeed the ministers favored by the Lord of the Rākṣasas;
O Monarch, they do not abandon the Lord of Laṅkā even in the face of life-threatening calamity. (20)
Therefore, let Your Majesty decree the appropriate punishment.
Rāma:—Vibhīṣaṇa! Do not say such a thing!
"By the mere command of these two, neither my own growth nor the destruction of the Lord of the Rākṣasas will occur; therefore, release them."
Lakṣmaṇa:
If he should release it, let my lord enter the entire camp, investigate, and then order its release.
Rāma: [Silence.]
"What Lakṣmaṇa has said is perfectly stated. Nīla! Let it be done so.
Nīla:
"As the Lord commands."
Rāma:
Or rather, come here for a moment.
Both: [They approach.]
These are they.
Rāma:
Let that lord of the rākṣasas be addressed in my name.
Having taken up this conflict myself by the abduction of my wife, I have come here desiring to see you; I do not see you, though I am a guest to the battlefield.
Thus.
Both:
As the King commands. (They both exit.)
Rāma:— Vibhīṣaṇa! We too shall first examine the army that is immediately adjacent.
Vibhīṣaṇa:—
"As the King commands.
Rāma—(walking about and looking around)—Ah! The venerable Sun has set. For now:
Having reached the summit of the western mountain and withdrawn his rays,
the sun appears with a body colored by the twilight,
like the frontal globe of an elephant draped in a garment of brilliant red silk.
Just like a thrill of joy produced by gold from the Jambu river. || 23 ||

Moreover: "The heroes headed by Prahasta and led by Kumbhakarṇa have been slain today by Rāghava, and even Śakrajit has emerged [from the battle]. (2) Even though things have come to this pass, he—under the sway of passion, disregarding even the words of his ministers, and considering himself a hero—desiring to fight, does not give up the daughter of Janaka, the queen of that bull of the Raghu dynasty. (3) (Entering) Vidyutjihva: Is my noble lord well? Chamberlain: Yes.
Vidyujjihva! Go; by the command of the Great King, let a likeness of the heads of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa be brought here. Vidyujjihva:
As the Great King commands. (Exit. Chamberlain:—
"Until I, too, shall become an intermediary for the Great King. (Exit. Interlude. (Then enters Sītā, surrounded by a host of Rākṣasa women.
Sītā:

"Indeed, why has there arisen today such a surge of agitation in my heart, which was so recently gladdened by the arrival of my noble lord? Furthermore, inauspicious omens are being seen. Even so, now—(is this some excess?)—a great increase, as if a great prosperity, expands within my heart. In every way, may the lords grant protection! (Indeed, why has there arisen today such a surge of agitation in my heart, which was so recently gladdened by the arrival of my noble lord? Furthermore, inauspicious omens are being seen.)

"Even so, now the great prosperity of my heart increases. May the lords grant peace in every way. (Then Rāvaṇa enters. Rāvaṇa: Stop, stop! This woman has departed from my palace, her hands still wet with the fresh water of the *amalaka* fruit. For when Laṅkā fell under my power in battle, she was seized immediately after I had swiftly conquered the descendant of Pulastya. Lady, stay, stay! You must certainly not go away. What do you say?

"I shall abandon you and go to Rāma! "Ah, you wretch! You were seized by force back then in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa; I shall seize you by force once more after slaying the descendant of Raghu in battle! What is the use of her? I too shall entice Sītā. (Manifesting the onset of passion) Oh, how incomparable is the power of the flower-bowed god!

Why is this? My eyes forget sleep at night upon beholding the face of Sītā; my exceedingly slender body, yearning for the joy of her embrace, has turned pale; and my fever is fixed upon lovely objects by the flower-arrowed god [Kāma]. Alas! Rāvaṇa, who has conquered the three worlds, is now being conquered by that very god. (Approaching) Sītā! O you with eyes like lotus petals, abandon this heart set upon a mortal, O mistress of my heart!
Behold today in battle your lover, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, as he is struck down by my weapon.
Sītā:
Ah, you are indeed a fool, O Rāvaṇa, you who desire to weigh Mount Mandara with your hand! (Entering) Rākṣasa: —
Victory to the Great King! These are the heads of those two human princes; having slain them in battle, the prince, desiring to please you, has taken them.
Rāvaṇa:
Sītā! Look, look at the heads of those two humans!
Sītā: [Gazes]
"Alas, noble husband! (She faints and falls. (Alas, noble husband!
Rāvaṇa:
Sītā! Abandoning your affection for this mortal whose life is spent, O large-eyed one, attain great glory this very day! 9.

Sītā—(Recognizing him) Alas, noble husband! Seeing your face, which resembles a freshly blossomed lotus, with its eyes turned away, I, unfortunate as I am, have indeed become utterly helpless. Alas, noble husband! Having cast me into this ocean of sorrow, where have you gone? Since I do not die, could this possibly be a falsehood? Noble sir! Kill me too with that very sword by which such an incomparable deed was done against my noble husband.

(Alas, noble son! Looking upon your face, which resembles a fresh, fragrant lotus, with its rolling eyes, I, unfortunate as I am, have indeed become utterly callous. Alas, noble son! Kill me as well with that very sword by which such an unworthy act was committed against my noble son! Rāvaṇa:
"Clearly, once that lowest of men has been slain in battle by Indrajit, whom will you have left to rescue you along with your brother Lakṣmaṇa? (Offstage) "By Rāma! By Rāma!
Sītā: "May you live long! (Entering)
Rākṣasa:—(With agitation) By Rāma! By Rāma! Rāvaṇa:—
"How? How was it by Rāma?

Rāvaṇa: Speak, speak! What has been done by that human ascetic? Rākṣasa:

The Great King ought to hear this: indeed, by that Rāghava, who possesses exalted courage and great strength, your son has been swiftly overcome and forcibly slain in battle today along with Lakṣmaṇa, O Lord of Laṅkā.
Rāvaṇa:

Ah, you evil-souled one! You coward in battle! Even he by whom the gods, including Indra, were conquered and the Daityas were turned back in flight—even that Indrajit is being slain in combat by a mere human!
Rākṣasa:
May the Great King be gracious, may he be gracious! No falsehood is spoken in the presence of the Great King’s feet except for the sake of the Prince. Rāvaṇa:
"Alas, my child Meghanāda! (Thus he falls, fainting.
Rākṣasa:
"Great King, take heart, take heart!"

Rāvaṇa:—(Recognizing him) Alas, my child! O you who caused fever to all the worlds! O master of weapons! Alas, my child! O conqueror of Indra, subduer of the circle of enemies! Alas, my child! O hero! O lover of your elders! O you who are fierce in battle! Alas, my child! Why have you departed from here, leaving me behind? (He faints. Rākṣasa:—
"Alas, what a tragedy! The Lord of Laṅkā, the conqueror of the three worlds, has been reduced to this state by that wretched Fate! O Great King, take heart, take heart!

Rāvaṇa:—(Recovering) Now, what is the use of this Sītā, who is the cause of my misfortune, or of this fickle Fortune, whose victory over the three worlds has become fruitless? (Falls down from grief.)"

Rākṣasa: Alas, O heroes of the night-stalkers! Since this has happened to the King, you guards stationed within the inner chambers must remain vigilant. (Offstage) Ho there, heroes of the night-stalkers! You who have turned away in terror, struck with fear by the ocean of a shattered army following the defeat of Prahasta, Nikumbha, Kumbhakarṇa, and Indrajit at the front of the battle! Continuous flight is unbecoming for you, who have repeatedly conquered the hosts of the gods; and yet, here stands your Lord, the Sovereign of Laṅkā, endowed with twenty arms and renowned for his victory over the entire world.
Rāvaṇa:
(Hearing this, with indignation) Go; let the news be ascertained further.
Rākṣasa: [Exit.]

"As the Great King commands. (Exit and re-enter) Victory to the Great King! Rāvaṇa:—(Rising suddenly with wrath) Where is he? Where is he? (Brandishing his sword) This sword, with its blade as hard as that which cleaves the frontal globes of Indra’s elephant, shall offer you as a sacrifice to my anger! Rākṣasa:— Great King! Enough of this extreme rashness!
Sītā:—
"Since Rāvaṇa is now performing such undesirable, unworthy, and ill-omened acts, his death will soon come to pass.

"For her sake, many of my brothers, sons, and friends have been slain. Rākṣasa:

May the Great King be gracious, may he be gracious! Enough, enough now of this incessant and futile exertion, which is devoid of any arrogance on the part of the enemy's forces. Furthermore, the killing of a woman must certainly not be committed.
Rāvaṇa:—
"In that case, bring the chariot.

Rāvaṇa:—(Mounting his chariot) O Sītā, today you shall behold Rāghava surrounded by the gods, his mind overwhelmed by the sharp arrows discharged from my bow. (Rāvaṇa exits with his retinue.
Sītā:—
"O Lords! If I follow my noble lord with a conduct worthy of my own lineage, may victory be unto my noble lord! (Exit. The Fifth Act.

First Actor:
"Of him whose banner is the vast and brilliant splendor of the Ikṣvāku lineage..."
The second [refers to] Rāma, who has made an effort for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa;

With our minds bound by curiosity to witness the battle,

Both: [They do so.]
"Very well. (Having done so) The First:

"Oh, how truly terrifying this battlefield appears! For here, strewn with the water that is the bodies of night-stalkers, possessing the waves that are the foremost of monkeys, and containing the crocodiles that are excellent swords, this battlefield shines like the ocean, its momentum increased by the rays of the moon-like arrow of the best of the Raghus."
The second [speaker] said:

"It is even so. These hosts of Rākṣasas have been struck down in battle like mountains shattered by thunderbolts; their heads broken by trees and boulders, they were slain with blows of the fists by the exceedingly powerful monkey leaders who were enraged, their tails and ears erect. With faces featuring wide-open eyes fixed upon their necks and fierce fangs at their lips, the throngs of demons were swiftly cast down."
The third [verse]:

"And these too must be observed by you both—Rākṣasas with sharp, stainless swords, their eyes wide with rage, possessing spotless and distorted fangs, resembling dark blue clouds; desiring to slay the army of the Lord of the Monkey hosts, they swoop down from all sides with mouths opened in fury. (4)
First:
"Oh, indeed! Arrows are being discharged by the Rākṣasas at the monkeys.

Mountains are hurled by the monkeys at the Nairṛtas;
the third [method]—
by the hurling of fists and the clashing of knees.

"May you both behold Rāvaṇa as well—brandishing a spear with a golden shaft, his pure fangs bared, driving his chariot; like the lord of the planetary spheres, the full-orbed moon appearing amidst the peak of the sunrise mountain, yet enraged at Rāma."
The second [verse]:

"May you two also behold Rāma—holding his bow in his left hand and turning a choice arrow with his other hand, standing on the ground while gazing at his enemy stationed in his chariot, like Kārttikeya in battle looking toward Mount Krauñca, the best of mountains. (7)
The third [speaker]:
Hahaha! This spear, resembling Time the Destroyer, was released by Rāvaṇa; it has been split in two by Rāma with his bow as he smiles.
First—Seeing Śakti struck down, Rāvaṇa, his eyes dilated with rage, rained a shower of arrows back at Rāma. || 9 ||

The third [speaker]:— Here he is, here he is! Raising his sharp bow fashioned with gold and swiftly brandishing a most terrible volley of arrows at the head of the battle, he approaches on foot the chariot-mounted Rāvaṇa, like a lion with sharp fangs approaching an intoxicated lord of elephants. (19)
All:— Ah! This region seems as if it were ablaze with light. What indeed could this be?

A chariot driven by Mātali was sent by Mahendra, who was apprehensive due to the commonality of their combat.
Second—
seeing that Mātali had arrived, Rāma ascended the chariot at his word.

Indeed, this chariot, which destroys the pride of the best of gods in battle and brings about the destruction of the sons of Diti, shines forth like the matted-haired Śiva of old, who was the cause of the destruction of the night-stalkers for the sake of slaying Tripura. 12.
First:

Oh, what a great battle has commenced! Having witnessed the combat between the best of men and the lord of the Nairṛtas, in which fierce arrows were swallowed by showers of shafts, these soldiers of the monkey-leader and the Rākṣasa host now stand with the falling of various weapons ceased. (13)

The second [actor]: Oh, indeed! These two, standing upon their chariot and revolving with their attendants, vomiting forth volleys of arrows, scorching the earth with the nets of their own rays, are like two suns wandering in the sky. (14)

"May you two also behold Rāvaṇa—he who, having crushed the horses with arrows of terrifying velocity and quickly struck down the banner with his might, is discharging a great rain of shafts, roaring, laughing, and causing intense terror to that god among men. (15)
First Actor:

This is indeed Rāma; having somewhat recovered after his body was dwarfed by the crushing of the [Daitya’s] position, with eyes bloodshot from gazing upon the fierce arrow and possessing the brilliance of the midday sun, the heroic king—having been granted a place on the chariot by Mātali himself—is enraged and has taken up the immeasurable, supreme weapon of the Grandfather (Brahmā). || 16 ||
The second [verse]:

"This weapon, released with the force of the arms of the best of the Raghus, possessing a sharp edge like the blazing sun, having slain the foremost of the night-stalkers in battle, returns again swiftly to Rāma himself. (17)
All:
Ah! Rāvaṇa has been struck down.
First:
Seeing Rāvaṇa slain, a rain of flowers was showered down; these drums of the dwellers of the three heavens resound deeply.
Second:
Very well; the task for the gods is accomplished.
First:
Therefore, please come. We too shall first pay our respects to Rāma, who is the benefactor of all. Both:—Certainly; that is the primary course of action. (All exit. Interlude. (Then enters Rāma.)
Rāma:

Having slain Rāvaṇa in battle today, swiftly afflicted by the force of my arrows, and having established the auspicious-minded Vibhīṣaṇa as the lord of Laṅkā; and having thus crossed, with my two arms, the ocean of my vow—a feat requiring no small courage—I now approach Laṅkā together with my kinsmen to comfort Sītā. (Entering) Lakṣmaṇa:
Victory to the Noble One! Noble One, here is the Noble Lady approaching your presence.
Rāma:
Child Lakṣmaṇa! Indeed, because Vaidehī has now been seen after having dwelt in the abode of the enemy, my indignation shall restrain my impatience.
Lakṣmaṇa: As the Noble One commands!
(Exit.)
(Entering) Vibhīṣaṇa:

Victory to the Lord! For here, O King, is your lawful wife, her sorrows dispelled by the prowess of your arm; she has returned through your grace, like the Goddess Lakṣmī who had previously fallen from the race of the Daityas. (21)

Rāma:—Vibhīṣaṇa! Let her remain right there for now, she who has been stained by contact with the night-stalkers, yet remains the very ornament of the Ikṣvāku dynasty. O Lord of Laṅkā, it is not fitting for you to look upon me while thinking of King Daśaratha as your father. Moreover: "O King, he who restrains a man sinking into unrighteous acts and worldly objects is indeed a friend; otherwise, he is an enemy. (22)
Vibhīṣaṇa:
May the Lord be gracious.
Rāma:—

"You ought not to cause further distress. (Entering) Lakṣmaṇa: "May my noble brother be victorious! Having heard your noble brother's intention, the noble lady awaits your favor for the sake of entering the fire. Rāma:
"Lakṣmaṇa! Fulfill the wish of this devoted wife.

Lakṣmaṇa: "As my noble brother commands. (Walking about) Alas! How painful! Having learned of the Queen’s purity and having heard my noble brother’s command, my mind, placed between duty and affection, wavers. (23) Who is there?
Hanumān: Victory to the Prince! Lakṣmaṇa: [Listens.]
"O Hanūmān! If you have the power, so commands the Noble One.
Hanūmān:
"In this matter, what does the Prince surmise?"
Lakṣmaṇa:
My reasoning has proven fruitless; or rather, we must follow the intention of our noble brother. Hanumān: [Agrees.]
"As the Prince commands. (They both exit.

(Entering) Lakṣmaṇa: May my noble brother be appeased. Noble brother! It is a marvel! For this noble lady—resembling a garland of blooming *śatapatra* lotuses, having quickly abandoned all hope for life here before the fire—having rendered your efforts here fruitless, enters [the fire] just as a female swan enters a lotus grove. (24)
Rāma:— A marvel, a marvel! Lakṣmaṇa! Hold him back, hold him back!
Lakṣmaṇa:—
"As the noble one commands.
Hanumān:
Victory to the Lord! This [Sītā], like a golden garland whose radiance has increased from the fire, having reached the purifier (Agni), has emerged unaltered, purified. (25)
Rāma—(with astonishment) What is it? What is it?
Lakṣmaṇa—
Oh, what a marvel! (Entering) Sugrīva:
Victory to the Lord! Who indeed is this person, appearing so worthy of homage, who has emerged from the blazing fire, having taken up the daughter of Janaka while she was still alive? 26.
Lakṣmaṇa:
Ah! Here comes the venerable Vibhāvasu (the Fire-god), preceded by the Noble Lady.
Rāma: [Observes]
Ah, this is the blessed Fire-god! Let us approach him now. (All approach. (Then Agni enters, carrying Sītā.
Agni:
This is the blessed Nārāyaṇa. Victory to the Lord!
Rāma:
O Blessed One! Salutations to you! Agni:—

"The Lord of the Gods ought not to pay homage to me. O Indra among kings! Accept this Jānakī, who is honored by all the worlds—sinless, uninjured, and pure, O Supreme Person! Furthermore, know that this divine Lakṣmī is the daughter of Janaka; she has come to you, having assumed a human body."
Rāma:

I am favored. O Fire-god, although I was already aware of Vaidehī’s purity, I acted in this very manner solely for the sake of convincing the world. (From behind the scenes, divine Gandharvas sing: Salutations to the Blessed Nārāyaṇa, the cause of the three worlds! O Lord of the three worlds, Brahmā is your heart; Rudra is your anger; the moon and sun are your eyes; and Bhāratī is your tongue, O Lord of the gods!

"O Lord, the three worlds, including Brahmā and the hosts of Maruts, were created by you alone! This Sītā is devoted to her home in the waters; you are Viṣṇu—please accept her! (30) (Again, behind the scenes, others sing: "O Agni, this earth was indeed lifted from the water by you in the form of a boar; O Lord of the Gods, the three worlds were traversed by you with three strides.
Yet, when you assumed your own form at will, the gods were not so comforted as they are now, having seen you slay Rāvaṇa in battle. (31)
Agni:— O gentle-faced one! These hosts of gods, celestial sages, perfected beings, knowledge-holders, gandharvas, and apsarases are honoring you with their respective splendors.
Rāma:—
I am favored. Agni:—
O gentle-faced one, come this way, this way, for the sake of the consecration.

Rāma: As the Blessed One commands. (Both exit. (Behind the scenes: Victory to the Lord! Victory to the Master! Victory to the Noble-faced One! Victory to the Great King! Victory to the Destroyer of Rāvaṇa! Victory to the Long-lived One! Vibhīṣaṇa:—

"Here he is, O Great King! Having crossed the ocean of his vow in battle today and having obtained the Goddess who is cleansed of all sin, he shines—having been consecrated by all the gods—like the moon in a clear sky. (32)
Lakṣmaṇa:

Oh, how truly resplendent is the Vaiṣṇava splendor of our noble brother! Surrounded by the hosts of gods, beginning with Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Vāsava, he shines forth, having performed his consecration at the command of Daśaratha.
"Having attained the sovereignty of the thirty gods, like Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra. (Then enters Rāma, consecrated, together with Sītā.
Rāma:

Child Lakṣmaṇa! By that king who, desiring the welfare of my mother, performed the *mitrābhiṣeka* (the friendly consecration) upon me—thereby making me the recipient of auspicious armlets and seating me upon the throne of honor—it is evident that he, having now gone to the state of the divine, has today once again, with a joyful mind, performed this very same consecration for me in person.
Agni:— O gentle-faced one! By the command of Mahendra, these subjects, led by Bharata and Śatrughna, have presented themselves before you.
Rāma:—
"Blessed One! I am overjoyed.
Agni—these Mahendra and others, the consumers of nectar, offer their salutations to you."
Rāma:
I am favored. Agni:—
"O gentle-faced one! What further favor may I bestow upon you?
Rāma:

"If the Blessed One is pleased with me, what more could I possibly desire? (Bharata’s Benediction: "May the cows be free from dust; may the enemy's army be pacified; and may this entire earth be ruled by our lion among kings. (All exit.)
The sixth act. The Abhiṣekanāṭaka is completed.
